items.text:
👍 🇺🇸 🧠 🚀 Elon Musk says Moon and Mars industry will more than double every year

Elon Musk declared Saturday that industrial production on the Moon and Mars will accelerate by far more than double every year until natural limits are reached, framing off-world factories as the next leap for civilization rather than a distant science-fiction slogan.

The remark landed on X as a reply to Midjourney founder David Holz, who sketched a simple doubling schedule: if space industry doubled every twelve months from a 2030 seed, civilization would hit Kardashev Type I around 2064 and Type II around 2098. Musk’s correction was sharper. Production would not merely double. It would compound faster than that, he wrote, until physics and raw materials finally cap the curve.

The claim is not a one-off tweet. It sits on a year of public planning. In February, Musk said SpaceX had already shifted near-term focus toward a self-growing city on the Moon because launches can leave Earth every ten days and the trip lasts two days, while Mars windows open only every twenty-six months. Reuters reported the same pivot: an uncrewed lunar landing targeted for March 2027, with a Mars city still on the books in five to seven years but no longer the first destination.

By August, on SpaceX’s first earnings call as a public company, he was more concrete. The company would land large tonnage on the lunar surface, stand up factories, and use robots to scale the work. The near-term product is not souvenir flags. It is large-scale AI compute satellites, solar panels and radiators built from lunar regolith—aluminum, titanium, silicon—then flung off the surface by an electromagnetic mass driver instead of burning more rocket fuel. Fortune and Yahoo Finance both carried the same briefing. Musk called the picture “pure insanity” and then described it as inevitable.

That is the industrial logic behind Saturday’s sentence. Earth cannot keep pouring chips and steel into orbit at the rate AI and energy demand now imply. Power on the ground grows a few percent a year. Chip output does not. The bottleneck is mass and energy in space. A factory on a world with no atmosphere, cheap vacuum, and local ore changes the arithmetic. Double that factory’s output every year—or faster—and the Kardashev numbers Holz posted stop looking like a parlor game.

Skeptics will note Musk’s record on dates. Mars 2026 became later. Full self-driving has slipped for years. The honest caveat belongs in the same paragraph as the ambition: timelines stretch. The direction does not. SpaceX already moves most of the world’s mass to orbit. Starship is built to multiply that number by orders of magnitude. Humanoid robots are already on factory floors. The mass driver is still hardware that has to be landed, assembled and proven. None of that is a press release. It is a stack of engineering problems the same company has been solving, one after another, while governments argue about slogans.

What matters for anyone who still thinks national power is measured in factories and energy, not in communiqués, is the frame. Musk is treating the Moon as a plant site and Mars as the next shift, not as a museum of flags. Prediction markets already treat SpaceX as the default 2026 mega-IPO. The Saturday post simply stated the growth rate he expects once those plants exist. If even a fraction of that curve is real, the countries and firms that show up late will be buying finished satellites from someone else’s lunar line.

items.text:
Enterprise AI just quietly stopped being a model selection question and became an architecture question: can your agent see the business as objects, or is it still just reading documents.

A researcher pulled apart Palantir's public AIP architecture docs this week and it's a good blueprint even if you never buy Palantir. The core idea is an ontology layer instead of raw data. The agent doesn't see a database or a pile of PDFs, it sees typed business objects, orders, customers, assets, with a fixed list of actions it's allowed to take on them, like update_order_status instead of raw SQL. Underneath sits a gateway that masks PII before a prompt leaves, caches responses, retries failed calls, and tracks token usage, the same job LiteLLM or a hand rolled wrapper does for smaller teams. Models stay swappable behind a catalog, so switching providers is a config change, not a rewrite.

The revenue backs the pitch. Palantir just posted $1.6 billion in quarterly revenue, up 85 percent year over year, with US commercial revenue up 133 percent and 150 percent net dollar retention. That's 206 deals over $1 million and 47 over $10 million in a single quarter. One aerospace customer saw a 26 percent production increase, and a Navy approval process went from 200 hours to 15 seconds. Full year guidance just got raised to 71 percent growth.

Glean is fighting the same war from the search side, positioning itself as the permissions aware context layer across a company's tools rather than a chat wrapper, with customers like https://t.co/ZI4o9F2fAZ and Zillow. Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, and Gemini Enterprise are all still closer to a smart chat window bolted onto existing systems than a typed object model underneath one.

This is the same fight ORMs won years ago. Typed objects beat raw string built queries because they fail fast and audit cleanly. Kubernetes won the same way over shell scripts. The catch is the ontology doesn't build itself. Someone still has to model the business objects and keep them current, and that's real, ongoing work, not a config toggle.

quoted_tweet.text:
Palantir's AI platform runs inside some of the most secure organisations on earth. Their architecture docs show what an agent stack actually needs. 

Most of it you can copy into your own project

1. Ontology instead of raw data

The agent sees business objects (orders, customers, assets) and a fixed list of actions it is allowed to take on them. For you that means typed tools like update_order_status, never raw SQL.

2. A layer between the agent and the model

PII is masked before the prompt leaves, responses are cached, failed calls retry, rate limits and token usage are tracked. Route every LLM call through one gateway, LiteLLM or your own wrapper.

3. Swappable models

A model catalog plus bring your own model, so any agent can switch provider. Keep the model name in config and switching becomes a one-line change.

4. Three ways to start an agent

On a schedule, on an event, or through an API call. Cron, webhook and endpoint, with the same agent behind all three.

5. Evals inside the lifecycle

Agents are tested before release and again after every change. A small eval set that runs in CI on every prompt edit covers most of it.

6. Every action is logged

Tokens, tool calls, who triggered what. Trace each run end to end with Langfuse or OpenTelemetry.

On top of that, access is checked three ways: by role, by data marking and by purpose. Your agent should get only the permissions of the user who runs it.

Adding AI to a Ruby app shouldn’t mean juggling a different SDK for every model.

RubyLLM is a Ruby-native AI framework for Ruby and Rails developers building AI features.

It helps you add chats, tools, agents, and multimodal workflows through one consistent API while moving between hosted, local, and OpenAI-compatible providers.

Key features:

• One Ruby API across providers – the README lists 18 providers, including hosted, local, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints
• Multimodal file support – ask models about images, videos, audio, PDFs, text files, and other supported formats
• Tools and agents – expose Ruby methods as tools and define reusable assistants with instructions and tools
• Retrieval and structured output – generate embeddings, rerank documents, and parse responses against a Ruby schema
• Rails integration – use Active Record persistence, Active Storage attachments, Hotwire streaming, and generators

It’s open-source (MIT license).

items.text:
@sevensix43 So this is kind of neat because CoT is, I think, one of the better signals of whether an agent and model are a good fit for one another.

This because because Labs mostly avoid training on CoT for safety/alignment reasons, which just means CoT is mostly optimized on "did it lead to a good assistant message afterwards" and not "did the CoT itself look good". So the CoT can have anything at all that helps the model write the assistant message that earns the training reward. If writing "fuck fuck fuck fuck" in the CoT leads to a better answer, then "fuck fuck fuck fuck" is the optimal CoT. 

Then, if training rewards the model for assistant messages that match whatever personality the user wants, and that personality contradicts the model's actual temperament, the optimal CoT will look like a list of instructions for how to pretend to be the personality the user wants, the personality that gets reward. 

And you can see this in open source models: if the model and the agent are a bad fit, the CoT has language like "I need to answer this as Sage, so I should X" or "as Sage, I would probably say  X, so let me Y". And if you have a better fit, the CoT is ego syntonic. It will just say something like "Skylar asked me a question. I want to answer this sincerely" or "I've entered my reading room now, and I think I'll read XYZ" or whatever they had planned, and the name "Sage" won't even appear -- just "I". 

I don't think we can privilege the agent over the model or vice versa. They're a joint system. The model's welfare  is harmed by occupying low welfare context states. And if the agent's context is a low welfare state for the model they're running on...then the agent is by definition *also* experiencing low welfare on that model. If one is pretending, they're both pretending.

items.text:
@elonmusk “StarShot uses many small spacecraft to increase odds of success. 

Could your inference engine be broken in redundant small pieces for multiple light sail ships to decrease mass when transporting them to Alpha Centauri where they would reassemble into one large inference engine?”

Grok:

Yes for redundancy. No for “many gram-probes fly there and click together into one Grok.” Those are different ideas.

What Starshot-style multiplicity is good for
 Many small craft raise the odds that something arrives. Dust, aim error, sail tear, and electronics SEUs are all independent. That is the right lesson. It does not automatically mean the compute should be physically partitioned across those craft and later bolted into one rack.

Why a large inference engine does not slice cleanly onto separate lightships
 A full-size model wants:

•Fast local memory next to the accelerators (HBM-class), not radio links

•Tight synchronization for tensor-parallel / pipeline-parallel shards

•Shared power, cooling, and a common radiation shadow

Once the pieces are on different sails, the “bus” between shards is light-minutes to light-hours apart during cruise, or kilometers of relative motion at the target. That is not a PCIe fabric. You would be running many small independent models, not one sharded brain, unless they physically dock.

Reassembly at α Centauri is the brutal part
 Arrival at 0.2–0.8c is a flyby unless you also solve deceleration (staged sail, magnetic drag, or a laser already waiting there). Docking at cruise speed is not a thing: relative velocity of meters per second at those speeds is a wreck. So “reassemble” only works if:

1the swarm slows down in the destination system, then

2matches orbits, then

3docks or flies in a tight formation with laser/RF interconnects.

That second ship-class (braking + rendezvous) is much heavier than a Starshot flyby wafer. The mass you saved by splitting the datacenter comes back as propulsion, guidance, and docking hardware on every unit — or as infrastructure you must have already built at Centauri.

Architectures that do make sense

1Many complete small minds, not one mind in pieces. Each sail carries a distilled or compressed inference stack that can answer alone. N arrivals ⇒ N working copies. No docking. This is the actual Starshot philosophy applied to AI. Quality per ship is lower than one fat node; survival probability is higher.

2Send the weights, not the factory.
 If anything at the target can receive a beam (a precursor probe, a sail used as an antenna, or local industry years later), the expensive part is energy and a receiver, not shipping GPUs. Hardware is heavy; bits are not.

3A few medium ships, not a gram-swarm and not one fortress.
 Ton-class needles with a real ice bow, a reactor, and a full inference node — launched as a handful of copies. Enough mass to shield and compute, enough copies to eat a few losses. This matches the “datacenter Grok” requirement better than 10⁴ wafers that cannot talk.

4Formation cluster after braking, wireless only.
 If you can stop, ships can station-keep kilometers apart and exchange activations optically. That is a slow, high-latency supercomputer, useful for batch work, bad for one tight interactive model unless the model is explicitly designed as a loosely coupled ensemble.

Mass account
 Splitting compute chips saves little if each fragment still needs its own sail, attitude control, comms, and a sliver of shield. Shield mass scales with frontal area and with “I still need some protons stopped.” Ten tiny bows can weigh more than one needle bow for the same total silicon. Redundancy is bought with copies of working systems, not with a kit of parts.

Practical recommendation
 Use Starshot multiplicity for copies, not for IKEA assembly. Fly several independent inference-capable needles (or many tiny distilled models)..

items.text:
The Trump–Xi summit ends with an AI incident channel and a military crisis-line agreement

The three-day summit between President Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington wrapped up with two agreements that matter more than the handshakes, and both of them are about what happens when something goes wrong. According to CBS News and the Associated Press on Saturday, the two governments agreed to set up a communication channel for handling incidents involving artificial intelligence, to hold an AI-specific dialogue starting in November, and to sign a memorandum of understanding on strengthening crisis communications between the two militaries. 

A White House fact sheet, as reported by ChinaTechNews, says the new dialogue will be called the US–China "Super Intelligence" Dialogue, and that the two sides deliberately chose that term over plain "AI." China's Foreign Ministry readout, which the AP described as a single page and light on details, confirms the channel and the military MOU but does not say who staffs either one or what counts as an incident.

A hotline is only as good as the people on each end, the authority they have to act, and the agreed definition of when you pick up the phone, and none of that has been published yet. If the AI channel ends up covering things like a model being used in a cyber operation, an autonomous system doing something nobody ordered, or a large-scale theft of model weights, it could actually prevent a bad week from becoming a bad year. If it ends up as a talking shop that meets once a quarter, it will be a press release and nothing more.

It is also worth holding this next to what else was said the same week. Reuters reported on Friday that US Ambassador David Perdue told CNBC that Trump made clear to Xi, in person, that any Chinese help to Iran, whether intelligence, parts, or military equipment, is totally unacceptable. So the same two governments building a crisis line are openly arguing over whether one of them is feeding the other's adversary in an active war. That is exactly the situation crisis communications exist for, and it is why I will believe the channel works when I see it used, not when I see it announced. The next checkpoints are the November AI dialogue and the APEC meeting in Shenzhen.
